title: Creating Reading Worksheets: From Real Text to Cambridge-Style Tasks
summary: Learn how to choose a real text and turn it into tasks like Exercises 1 to 4, with rules for good questions, a full worked example, a quality checklist and a way to test your worksheet.

sections.h: Why make your own reading tasks
p: Past papers are limited. You may use them all in one term. Students also need practice with topics that matter in their own lives. When you make tasks yourself, you can use local topics, current news and your students' level.
The key is to copy the Cambridge style so the practice matches the exam. This unit shows how.
Remember what the exam looks like (from Week 1):
• Exercise 1: a text of about 400 to 450 words. Six questions, short answers, last question asks for three details. 8 marks.
• Exercise 2: matching, a text of about 600 to 650 words in up to five sections, or up to five shorter texts. Nine questions. 9 marks.
• Exercise 3: notes completion from a text of about 400 to 500 words. 7 marks.
• Exercise 4: multiple choice, a text of about 550 to 600 words, six questions with options A, B, C. 6 marks.

b: Practice for topics you want to review.
A chance to bring local examples into the class.
A way to adjust difficulty for your students.
A model for students who later write their own questions.

p: Look for texts that students would actually read, and that are connected to the exam topics: technology, health, travel, environment, school life, jobs, hobbies, culture and festivals.
Where to look:
• Newspaper and magazine articles for young readers.
• Websites about science, nature or travel.
• School newsletters or notices.
• Your own writing. You can write a text for your class in 20 minutes.
How to check the text:
• Level: students should understand most words (about 90 to 95 percent) at a normal reading speed. A few new words should be guessable from context.
• Length: choose the length for the exercise, or use a shorter text for a first practice.
• Content: facts, opinions and details that give you good questions.
• Topic: respectful, clear and not too sensitive.
• Names, dates and numbers: not too many, unless you want them for questions.
Copyright: use short extracts for classroom teaching, name the source, and do not publish the text. If in doubt, write your own text or ask the author.

b: Can I write six good questions about it?
Are there ideas that can be paraphrased?
Is it too easy or too hard?
Is it safe and fair for my class?

p: Exercise 1 asks short answers. The answers are single words or short phrases from the text.
Rules for writing questions:
• Write five questions with one answer, and one question that needs three details.
• Put questions in the same order as the information in the text.
• Ask who, what, where, when, how and why. Avoid questions with 'yes' or 'no'.
• Make sure there is only one possible answer.
• Make questions use different words from the text to test understanding.
• Choose answers of one to four words.
Mark scheme tips:
• Write the correct answer and other acceptable answers.
• Use brackets for words that are not needed: '(the) head'.
• For the three-detail question, give four or five possible details so that students can choose any three.
The examiner report warns students not to add wrong information, and to be precise. For example, a question about the title of an event needs the key word 'World' in 'World Cosplay Summit'.

ex.t: A weak and a strong question
b: Weak: 'Is the plant easy to grow?' (yes or no).
Strong: 'What is the main source of water for plants without a long root?'

p: Exercise 2 asks students to match nine statements to sections of text or short texts.
Rules:
• Use up to five short texts or sections, A to E.
• Write nine statements. Each answer is one of the texts. Some texts can be used more than once.
• Write each statement using paraphrase, so students must understand meaning, not match words.
• Include some statements that test implied meaning, such as 'which person suggests...'.
• Make sure only one text fully fits each statement.
• Avoid giving the same exact words as the text.

The examiner report for June 2024 says students find it hard when the key word of the statement is 'suggests', or when two texts contain the same word. Your task should train students to read the whole paragraph and follow the discourse markers (but, however, although, because).

b: Text: 'I'll turn up whatever the weather, however cold or wet.'
Statement: 'Which person says they will go swimming whatever the weather?'

p: Exercise 3 asks students to complete notes under headings. Answers are short notes, not full sentences.
Rules:
• Choose a text with a list of ideas or two clear groups (for example, advantages and disadvantages).
• Write a heading and a note frame with a space for the answer.
• Say how many notes are needed: 'Give three points'.
• Make sure the heading controls what the answer must be. The notes must fit the heading, as the examiner report says.
• Write the answers in brief form, with a verb after the heading when the heading needs it.
Example heading: 'Ways cities can reduce traffic' and the note: 'charging drivers to enter parts of the city'. A note that says only 'charging drivers' lacks key meaning.
Mark scheme: list all acceptable notes and mark the essential words in capitals so markers can see what is needed.

b: Heading: Reasons people like tiny homes.
1 ______ (they can be moved easily).
2 ______ (people can get rid of things they do not need).

sections.h: Step 5: Write Exercise 4 style multiple choice
p: Exercise 4 has six multiple-choice questions with options A, B and C.
Rules:
• Write the stem as a clear question or an unfinished sentence.
• Write one correct option that fully answers the question.
• Write two distractors. Each distractor should be mentioned in the text but should not answer the question.
• Make the options the same length and grammar.
• Do not write 'all of the above' or 'none of the above'.
• Put the correct answer in different positions.
• Include one or two questions about implied meaning or the writer's opinion. Use words like 'suggests' or 'implies' in the stem.
How to check: ask a colleague to answer without the text. If they can guess the answer, the options are too obvious.
The examiner report says students often pick an option because one word matches the text. Plan distractors that use text words but give the wrong idea.

b: Stem: What does the writer suggest about people who cycle to work?
A They save money on fuel.
B They arrive at work earlier.
C They are healthier than drivers.
Only one is supported by the whole paragraph.

sections.h: A worked example: an original text and six questions
p: Here is a short text written for this course. It is shorter than an exam text. Use it to see the rules in action.

Text: The Return of the Bicycle. Twenty years ago, many cities were full of cars. Streets were noisy, the air was dirty and traffic moved slowly. Today, things are changing in some places. In a city called Riverton, the government built a network of safe cycle lanes. At first, many people said nobody would use them. However, within two years, the number of people riding to work had doubled. Shop owners were worried that customers would stop coming, but sales went up because people stopped to look in the windows. The city now plans to add 50 kilometres of new lanes by 2030. Not everyone is happy. Some drivers say the lanes make the roads too narrow. Even so, a recent survey found that three out of four residents support the plan.
Questions:
• 1. What was the problem in cities twenty years ago? (Answer: (too many) cars / traffic.)
• 2. What did the government of Riverton build? (Answer: (a network of) safe cycle lanes.)
• 3. How long did it take for the number of cyclists to double? (Answer: (within) two years.)
• 4. What did shop owners fear? (Answer: customers would stop coming.)
• 5. What is the plan for 2030? (Answer: 50 (kilometres) of new lanes.)

• 6. Give three details about how people feel about the lanes. (Answers: at first people said nobody would use them; shop owners worried; some drivers say roads are too narrow; three out of four residents support the plan.)

b: Questions are in the order of the text.
Answers are short.
There is one clear answer for each.
The last question gives four possible details for three marks.

sections.h: Quality checks before you use the worksheet
p: Always test your worksheet.
• Do it yourself without looking at your key. Do you get the same answers?
• Ask a colleague to do it. Where do they hesitate?
• Time it. Is it realistic for the lesson?
• Check each question: could there be two correct answers? Fix the question or add the second answer to the key.
• Write the key with acceptable alternatives and marks.
• Label each question with a skill code: R1 facts, R2 connections between ideas, R3 selecting details, R4 implied meaning.
• Print clearly, with a title and instructions in the same style as the exam.
After use, check the results. If most students miss one question, look at the question before blaming the students. Maybe it was unclear. Improve the worksheet and save the new version.

b: Add a pre-reading question to get students ready.
Add a post-reading task: 'Do you agree with the writer?'
Create two versions: a support one with glossary and a stretch one with an extra open question.

activity: Take the real text you brought. Choose one exercise type, write six or nine questions and the key. Swap with a colleague. Have them answer without your key and tell you where the questions were unclear. Improve your worksheet.

check.q: What should the options in a multiple-choice question be like?
o: One correct option and two distractors of similar length that are mentioned in the text

check.q: What is the best way to test your own worksheet?
o: Ask a colleague to do it and note where they hesitate
Give it to the whole class without checking

check.q: Why should a mark scheme show brackets, such as '(the) head'?
o: To show words that are not essential for the mark
To show the answer is wrong
To show the order of questions

title: Creating Speaking and Writing Prompts
summary: Write your own Paper 3 interview questions, Part 2 cards and Part 3 discussion questions, and your own Exercise 5 and Exercise 6 writing tasks, using the real patterns and a quality checklist.

p: Cambridge changes the cards and tasks each year. Students need many different practice prompts. When you write your own, you can match topics to your students' lives and you can practise each skill again and again.
A good prompt does four jobs:
• It is clear. Students know what to do.
• It is fair. It does not need special knowledge.
• It is open. It lets students say a lot.
• It matches the exam pattern. Students learn what to expect.

b: Read three real examples carefully.
Notice the exact wording.
Copy the pattern, not the words.

sections.h: Part 1 interview questions: the three-question pattern
p: Each Part 1 topic has three questions. They follow a pattern.
• Question 1: now or habits. 'Can you tell me something about...?' or 'How do you...?'
• Question 2: a past story. 'Can you tell me about a time when..., and what happened?'
• Question 3: an opinion or the future. 'Do you think...? Why? Why not?'
Original examples:

• Festivals: 1 What festivals do you celebrate with your family? 2 Can you tell me about a festival you enjoyed, and what happened? 3 Do you think festivals are important for a community? Why? Why not?
• Transport: 1 How do you usually travel in your town? 2 Can you tell me about a time when your journey went wrong, and what happened? 3 Do you think cities should have fewer cars? Why? Why not?

• Shopping: 1 Where do you usually buy your clothes? 2 Can you tell me about something you bought that you were happy with? 3 Do you think young people spend too much money on things they do not need? Why? Why not?
• School clubs: 1 Which clubs does your school have? 2 Can you tell me about a time when you took part in a club activity? 3 Should every student join a club? Why? Why not?
Keep the language simple. Avoid words that need special knowledge.

b: Choose a topic: music, pets, technology, weather, the internet, volunteering.
Write Q1 now, Q2 past, Q3 opinion.
Ask a student to answer and note if the tenses are used.

p: The card has a title, a context sentence, two options in bullet points and a task. The task asks students to talk about the options and say which one they prefer and why. The questions focus on how useful, how easy or difficult, how enjoyable, or the advantages and disadvantages.
Template:
• Title (two or three words).
• Context: 'Your school is planning a... You are considering the following options:'
• Option 1.
• Option 2.
• Task: 'Talk about how ... each option would be. Say which option you would prefer, and why.'
Original examples:

• Card 1: Learning a skill. Your friend wants to learn a new skill during the holidays. You are considering the following options: joining a cooking class; learning to play the guitar. Talk about how difficult each option would be. Say which option you would prefer, and why.

• Card 2: A school trip. Your class is planning a trip. You are considering the following options: visiting a science museum; spending a day at the beach. Talk about the advantages and disadvantages of each option. Say which option you would prefer, and why.

• Card 3: Helping at home. You want to help your family more. You are considering the following options: doing the cooking once a week; looking after your younger brother or sister after school. Talk about how easy or difficult each option would be. Say which option you would prefer, and why.

• Card 4: Keeping in touch. A friend has moved to another country. You are considering the following ways to stay in touch: sending messages every day; making a video call once a week. Talk about how useful each option would be. Say which option you would prefer, and why.

b: The two options are both realistic and equally easy to talk about.
There is no right answer.
The task words match the options (advantage, difficulty, enjoyment, usefulness).
The language level is easy to read in one minute.

p: Part 3 asks four or more questions connected to the Part 2 topic but wider. They ask for opinions and reasons. They often start with 'Do you think...', 'Some people say... What is your opinion?', 'Do you agree?' or 'What are the advantages and disadvantages of...?'
Original examples for the card 'A school trip':
• Some people say that school trips are a waste of time. What do you think?
• Do you think students learn more outside the classroom than inside? Why? Why not?
• What are the advantages and disadvantages of travelling in a large group?
• All students should visit a different country before they leave school. Do you agree?
Tips:
• Do not repeat what was in the card. Move to a larger idea.
• Mix agree/disagree statements with open questions.
• Make sure students of any background can answer.

b: Write four Part 3 questions for each of your four cards.
Try them with two students.
Which questions gave the longest answers?

sections.h: Writing tasks for Exercise 5: the informal email
p: Exercise 5 gives a situation, an instruction to write an email to a friend, three bullet points, and the word limit. The pattern from the 2024 specimen paper is:
• Situation: one or two sentences.
• Instruction: 'Write an email to a friend about...'.
• 'In your email you should:' with three bullet points.
• 'Write about 120 to 160 words.'
• 'You will receive up to 6 marks for the content of your email, and up to 9 marks for the language used.'
Original examples:
• You recently went to a concert. Write an email to a friend about it. Say why you went, describe what you saw and heard, and say if you would go again.
• You have started learning a new sport. Write an email to a friend about it. Explain why you chose the sport, describe your first lesson and say what you hope to achieve.
• Your school has a new student from another country. Write an email to a friend about the new student. Describe the student, say how you welcomed them and say what you plan to do together.
The bullets should cover: a reason, a description and a plan or a feeling. Make each bullet one clear task.

b: Is the reader a friend?
Are there exactly three bullets?
Is each bullet clear and possible to develop?
Is the word limit stated?

sections.h: Writing tasks for Exercise 6: formal writing with stimulus
p: Exercise 6 is a more formal piece. It may ask for an article, report, essay or review. It gives a situation, an instruction, a stimulus such as speech bubbles, and a request to use some of the ideas and add ideas of your own.

The 2024 specimen Question 17 shows this pattern: a class took part in a one-day sports festival. Students wrote a report that said what was enjoyable and suggested improvements, using four comments in speech bubbles.
Original examples:

• Report: Your school held a careers day. The organisers want students' opinions. Say what was useful and how it could be improved. Comments: 'I met people from different jobs'; 'The talks were too short'; 'There were not enough students at the talks'; 'I learned how to write a CV'.
• Article: Write an article for your school magazine about why young people should learn to cook. Comments: 'It saves money'; 'It is healthier'; 'It can be a fun hobby'; 'It takes too much time'.

• Review: Write a review of a film, book or app you recently tried. Say what was good, what was less good and whether you would recommend it. Comments: 'The story was exciting'; 'It was too long'; 'The pictures were beautiful'; 'It helped me practise English'.
• Essay: 'Students should be allowed to use phones in class.' Comments: 'Phones are useful for research'; 'They can distract students'; 'Some students have no phone'; 'Teachers should decide'.
Always ask for 120 to 160 words and give the marks for Content and Language.

b: Is the audience clear (organisers, readers, a teacher)?
Do the comments give ideas that can be extended?
Does the task need students to add their own ideas?
Is the register formal or semi-formal?

p: Once you have prompts, use them in different ways.
• Pair practice: one student asks, one answers, then swap.
• Speaking stations: set up three places with different cards. Students rotate every three minutes.
• Write after talk: students talk about the card, then write the same ideas as a report.
• Peer test: a student acts as the examiner and the partner takes the test. The third student marks with a checklist.
• Prompt bank: store them in a folder labelled by topic and level. Add a note about which worked best.
Share prompts with colleagues. Ask for new ideas each term. Keep a master copy with answers or sample responses.

b: Topic | Part 1 questions | Part 2 card | Part 3 questions | Writing task | Notes.
Add 3 new prompts every month.

activity: Write one complete speaking set (three Part 1 questions, one Part 2 card, four Part 3 questions) and one Exercise 5 email task and one Exercise 6 task. Test the speaking set with a student and the writing tasks with a colleague. Note what to improve.

check.q: What kind of question is Question 2 in a Part 1 set?
o: A question about a past event
A question about the present only

check.q: What should an Exercise 5 task have?
o: A situation, an email to a friend and three bullet points
A formal letter and no bullets

check.q: What is true of a good Part 2 card?
o: It has two realistic options and asks for a preference with a reason

title: Adapting Endorsed Materials: Scaffold, Stretch and Use Safely
summary: Learn what endorsed textbooks are, how to judge a textbook activity, five moves to adapt it, how to scaffold and extend, a worked example and how to use publishers' books within copyright rules.

p: Endorsed materials are books and resources that Cambridge has checked and approved as a good match for a syllabus. Publishers such as Cambridge University Press and Collins make them. They usually include a student's book, a workbook, a teacher's guide and audio.

For example, the Collins Cambridge IGCSE English as a Second Language Student's Book, third edition, is endorsed for examination from 2024. Always check the Cambridge website for the current list of endorsed resources for your syllabus year.
What endorsement means:
• The book follows the syllabus and the exam style.
• Cambridge has looked at the quality of the content.
What it does not mean:
• It does not mean the book is perfect for your class.
• It does not mean you must use every page.
• It does not replace the syllabus, the past papers or the mark schemes. The syllabus is always the main document.

b: Use the contents page to match units to your scheme of work.
Use the teacher's guide for ideas and keys.
Use the audio scripts after listening tasks.

sections.h: How to judge a textbook activity
p: Before you use an activity, ask these questions.
• Syllabus fit: which skill code does it practise (R1, W2, L2, S3)?
• Level: is it too easy or too hard for my class?
• Time: can I do it in the lesson?
• Interest: is the topic close to my students' life?
• Interaction: do students talk or write, or only fill gaps?
• Support: are there models, word lists, answers?
• Gaps: what is missing, such as speaking practice or feedback?
Give each activity a quick score: keep, change or skip.

b: A gap-fill on the past tense: keep but add a speaking task after it.
A very long reading with hard vocabulary: change by splitting it into two parts with a glossary.
A discussion topic that your students do not know: swap it for a local topic.

sections.h: Five moves to adapt an activity
p: There are five easy moves. Remember them as the five S's.
• Select: choose only the activities you need.
• Swap: change names, places and topics for local ones.
• Scaffold: add support so that more students can succeed.
• Stretch: add challenge for stronger students.
• Supplement: add a speaking or writing task, or a quick check, that the book does not give.

b: Which pages will I select?
What will I swap?
How will I scaffold?
How will I stretch?
What will I supplement?

p: To scaffold means to give temporary support, like the frame around a building. Remove it when students can work alone.
Ways to scaffold:
• Pre-teach key words before reading or listening.
• Give a model answer or a first example.
• Give sentence starters for speaking and writing.
• Divide a long task into small steps.
• Give a graphic organiser, such as a table or a spider diagram.
• Let students read or listen twice and compare answers in pairs.
• Offer hints or partly completed answers.
• Use pictures.
• Pair a stronger student with a student who needs support.
• Allow extra time.
Scaffolds should help students think, not give them the answers.

ex.t: A scaffold for a short talk
b: I'm going to talk about two options: ___ and ___.
The main advantage of ___ is that ___.
However, ___ because ___.
So overall I would choose ___ because ___.

p: Strong students need challenge too. Ways to stretch:
• Add an open question after a closed one: 'Why do you think the writer chose these words?'
• Ask for two or three reasons instead of one.
• Remove support, such as the word list or the model.
• Ask students to write their own questions about a text for a partner.
• Ask students to rewrite for a different audience (for example, a formal letter instead of an email).
• Add a time limit.
• Ask them to compare two texts.
• Ask them to give a short talk using the same material.

b: After a reading task, students write three questions for the next class.
After a listening task, students write a short email answering the speaker.

sections.h: A worked example of adapting one task
p: Imagine a textbook page with a reading about public transport and these tasks: read the text; answer six questions; discuss the question 'Do you use public transport?'
The class has mixed levels and little speaking practice. Here is how you could adapt.
• Select: keep the reading and the six questions.
• Swap: add a local bus route as a second short text.
• Scaffold: pre-teach six key words (commute, fare, ticket, platform, delay, schedule) and let students read twice and compare answers in pairs.
• Stretch: ask stronger students to write two more questions for a partner and to find the writer's opinion.

• Supplement: turn the discussion into a Part 2 style card: 'You are choosing between a bus and a bicycle to get to school. Talk about how useful each option would be. Say which you would prefer, and why.'
Result: the same page now gives reading practice, vocabulary, speaking and a clear exam link.

b: Planning: about 20 minutes.
Preparing a glossary and a card: 10 minutes.
The result can be reused every year.

p: Textbooks and audio are protected by copyright. Respect it to protect authors and to keep your school safe.
• Read your school's licence and the publisher's terms. They may allow limited copying for classroom use.
• Do not copy whole books or share them online.
• Do not post audio or scripts in public places.
• When you adapt, make your own new version, not a copy of the publisher's pages.
• Always write the source on worksheets (for example, 'Adapted from ...').
• Use free official resources from Cambridge, such as past papers and the examiner reports on the Cambridge website, as they allow.
• Keep confidential exam materials, such as live speaking cards, secure.
If you are unsure, ask your head of department or the publisher.

b: Do I have permission to copy?
Is my version new and different?
Is the source written down?
Is anything confidential?

sections.h: Mapping a book to your scheme of work
p: Use your four-column scheme to plan with the book. Put the unit pages into Column 2 and Column 3. Then look for gaps.
• Does the book give enough practice for Paper 3 Part 2 and Part 3?
• Is there enough exam-style writing?
• Are there enough listening tasks of the Cambridge style?
• Are mark schemes or criteria included?
Add your own tasks to fill the gaps. Cross out the activities you will skip. Share the map with colleagues so everyone teaches the course in the same way.

b: Unit | Pages | Syllabus skill | Keep, change or skip | My addition.

activity: Choose one page from a textbook or a past paper. Judge it with the seven questions. Then adapt it with the five S's, write the changes and use it in class. Note what happened.

o: Give temporary support that you take away as students improve

check.q: What does endorsement by Cambridge NOT mean?
o: The book is perfect for every class and replaces the syllabus
The book follows the exam style
